newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Czech trade gap jumps but positive trend seen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Czech trade gap jumps but positive trend seen.

text.p: The Czech trade deficit for the first two months of 1997 nearly doubled year-on-year, but analysts said it still showed a favourable trend for sagging exports and was largely in line with expectations.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) on Monday said the February trade gap was 13.7 billion crowns ($468.4 million), pushing the January-February shortfall to 27.2 billion crowns, up from 16.2 billion over the first two months of 1995.
"The figures are slightly better than expected," said Vladimir Kreidl, an economist at Patria Finance. A Reuters poll of economists had forecast a 14.5 billion crown gap for February.
Kamil Janacek, chief economist at Komercni Banka, said the deficit for the full-year remained on track to meet forecasts of under or around 200 billion crowns.
The CSU forecast a trade deficit of 211-219 billion crowns for 1997 after a record 160.3 billion crown gap in 1996.
Imports over the two months totalled 123.1 billion crowns, a 9.1 percent year-on-year increase, while exports contracted 0.7 percent to 95.9 billion crowns, the bureau said in a statement.
Janacek noted that despite the decline in exports, the figure was an improvement over January when exports shrunk by some 2.5 percent.
"There is a slight improvement for exports. I think that we can expect a recovery in exports from the second quarter of the year," he said.
Imports of raw materials and machinery remained at the heart of the deficit, accounting for some 81 percent of the goods brought into the country, the CSU added.

Analysts said this figure was to be expected as industry underwent major restructuring, although it remained to be seen if the imports were being used efficiently and would translate into economic growth.
"There is no space for saying that everything is okay (because of the January-February results)," said Kreidl. "This single figure doesn't change anything. It's only slightly better than expected."

The trade figures followed better than expected gross domestic product (GDP) figures. Fourth quarter 1996 GDP rose 4.7 percent, reversing a steady downtrend from the first quarter which had prompted calls for an interest rate cut to stimulate the economy.

The Czech crown strengthened slightly on the trade data, rising some 40-50 basis points to around 1.4 percent above its dollar/mark basket parity. The central bank fixed the crown on Monday at 1.32 percent above parity, up from 0.88 percent on Friday.
"The trade figures are in line with what we expected. (But) the CNB (Czech National Bank) will definitely not cut interest rates," said Petr Tomek, a foreign exchange dealer at Zivnostenska Banka.
The CNB last increased its key interest rate, the discount rate, last summer as part of a series of tightening moves to choke a rapidly growing money supply and ease inflation.
The discount rate was raised one percentage point to 10.5 percent. At the same time, the CNB raised repo rates and pushed up the minimum reserve requirements to 11.5 percent from 8.5 percent.

The moves appear to be working, with M2 money supply -- which measures currency, demand deposits, time and savings deposits, and foreign currency deposits -- easing to 7.8 percent in December from 20.2 percent in the same month of 1995.
In addition, inflation has continued its gradual easing, dipping to 7.3 percent year-on-year in February. ($ = 29.25 Czech Crowns)
